title: 5TH ANNUAL NC VETERAN ART SHOW
location: Durham Art Guild, DAG Golden Belt Gallery, Mill No. 1 at Golden Belt Campus, 800 Taylor St., Durham, 27701
description:
Please join us for the 5th Annual North Carolina Veteran Art Show from Friday, October 2nd, to Friday, October 16th, at the Durham Art Guild Golden Belt Gallery.  The Joel Fund and Heart2Hand Veteran artist Lt. Colonel (retired), Bernardine Donato, are excited to host the two-week art exhibit in partnership with Durham Art Guild. This family-friendly art show will contain original pieces created by North Carolina Veterans of all backgrounds, art levels, and branches of service. 
To learn more and submit artwork until September 14th, please visit: thejoelfund.org/nc-veteran-art-show/ 
Gallery Hours:
Monday – Saturday, 10 am – 7 pm
Sunday, 12 pm – 4 pm
There is free, paved parking on site with an accessible entrance. 
During the Third Friday Durham Art Walk, an Artist Talk and Closing Reception is planned for October 16th, from 6:00-7:15 pm, with light refreshments until 8:00 pm. This event is designed to foster community engagement and honor the service and artistic talent of North Carolina veterans. The structured program, from 6:00 PM to 7:15 PM, will feature a moderated Artist Talk panel, audience Q&A, an art tour, and a meet and greet with veteran artists. Please visit this website to see the other events and galleries that are open for the evening! https://downtowndurham.com/thirdfriday-2/ 
Can’t make it in person? The featured artwork will be on The Joel Fund’s Operation ART Online Gallery, as well as an online gallery on the DAG website. Click here to see DAG Gallery at Golden Belt. 
If you have any questions, please contact Isabella Brezenski
at 919-200-0886 or via email at isabella@thejoelfund.org.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Open Studio: Glass & Other
location: Fusion Gallery, 321 W Main St, Durham, 27701, United States
description:
Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM. 
Use our studio space and tools or bring your own project to work on; perfect for artists who don’t have a home studio or simply want dedicated time and space to make. Personal cubbies are also available to store works-in-progress between visits. 
Online registration or sign-up via email is required before coming in. Drop-ins are not permitted at this time. If you’d like to come in at a time you don’t see available online, email us at info@fusionnc.com. 
How Open Studio Works
Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction. You should already have the skills needed to safely work in your chosen medium. It’s also a great opportunity to finish projects started during a Fusion class. 
Your Day Pass includes access to our shared workspace, tools, equipment, and currently available non-consumable materials. Consumable and specialty materials are charged separately based on usage. 
Stained & Fused Glass
Prior stained or fused glass experience is required to use our glass tools. Taking a basics or beginner class at Fusion is recommended, but previous instruction at Carolina Stained Glass or Say It With Glass is also accepted. 
• Glass, solder, foil, and frit: $35/lb
• Bringing your own stained glass? Foil and solder use: $6
• Paper stained glass patterns: Free
• Vinyl-cut patterns: $3 each
• An assortment of stained glass patterns is available for studio use
• Kiln firings are handled by Fusion staff only 
Silver Clay
Prior silver clay experience is required to use silver clay tools. Taking a beginner class at Fusion is recommended before using the studio independently. 
• Silver clay: $7/gram prior to firing
• Firing of your completed piece is included and will be completed at the convenience of Fusion studio staff
• Guests may not fire their own pieces without prior authorization from Fusion’s owners 
Drawing & Painting
No prior class or experience is required for drawing or painting. Your Open Studio fee includes access to currently available shared drawing and painting materials. 
Please Note
• Day Pass access is valid 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected date only
• Online or email registration is required before arriving—no walk-ins
• Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction
• Some specialty tools, equipment, or processes may require prior approval or demonstrated experience
• Guests are responsible for cleaning their workspace and helping maintain a respectful shared environment
• Misuse of the space, tools, or equipment or failure to follow studio guidelines may result in removal from the studio without refund

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: AGS: Yorktown Staff Ride
location: None
description:
On October 3 and 4, the Program in American Grand Strategy will hold our annual staff ride - this year to Yorktown, Virginia, site of the final major campaign of the American Revolutionary War.

2026 marks the 250th anniversary of American independence, and the Yorktown campaign of 1781 is the hinge on which that independence turned. Without Washington and Rochambeau's audacious march south, without the French fleet's decisive victory at the Battle of the Capes, and without the siege that forced Cornwallis's surrender, there might be no United States. There is no better moment to walk this ground.

A staff ride is a hands-on educational experience where participants walk the terrain of a battle or campaign. Participants will visit the battlefield and deliver a presentation from the perspective of an individual involved in the Yorktown Campaign - drawn from a cast of historical figures that includes American commanders, French allies, British generals and ministers, a private soldier, a camp follower, and an enslaved man who escaped to the British lines in search of the freedom the Revolution promised but did not yet deliver.

Students are encouraged to apply regardless of program of study, year, or prior involvement with AGS. We are looking for students interested in and willing to participate in an exciting learning exercise on the American Revolution, focusing on the Yorktown Campaign of 1781. No specific expertise is required.

AGS will cover all travel and lodging costs for participants, along with meals. Students will be responsible for any recreational expenses outside of the staff ride's program.

Join us for a mindful walk at beautiful Johnston Mill Preserve!
 

This forest bathing style meditation does not require clearing your mind of thoughts, sitting motionless, or focusing on your breath. Certified mindfulness meditation teacher Barbara Shumannfang will guide a variety of meditations for you to try, ending with tips on how to apply mindfulness in your daily life. Questions? Contact Barbara at bshumannfang@gmail.com. This is a free event but preregistration is required.

title: Remembering in the Garden: Community Journaling in Nature
location: Duke Gardens–Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
In this community journaling in nature workshop, explore ways that gardens and stories can heal our minds and bodies. On a guided, meditative stroll amongst the grand and small sights, sounds and smells of Duke Gardens, you will be invited to notice, feel and remember. Dr. Zelda Lockhart, author, expressive arts therapist and Fulbright Specialist, will offer prompts to journal, draw and reconnect to each other and the natural ecology of the living and the dead. This workshop will offer activities that can be integrated as daily practice wherever you live and wherever you go, toward the goal of individual, ancestral and community healing. 
Presenter’s Bio: Dr. Zelda Lockhart is a current Fulbright Specialist who holds a PhD in Expressive Arts Therapies. Her novels, keynotes and workshops focus on the power of story and nature to connect us across boundaries constructed by colonialism and heal our generations from the wounds of colonialism. Visit her website at www.zeldalockhart.com. 
Fee: $28; 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Parking fees apply. 
Location: Meet at the Barnes Welcome Center. 
Accessibility: This program takes place partially seated indoors and partially outdoors, traveling on a combination of paved and unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and moderate inclines and outdoor seating on stone or grass surfaces. The indoor location is equipped with a hearing loop, which transmits sound directly to hearing aids and cochlear implants with a T-coil setting. Accessible restrooms are available onsite.

title: Turbo Tarot
location: Center for Documentary Studies
description:
Join us for a second free public event with visiting artist Kenya (Robinson), following her October 3 performance, "Fluid Master."

Using the first edition of TURBO TAROT, Kenya explores the integrated systems of a passenger vehicle through the symbolic framework of the tarot. Blending automotive maintenance, philosophy, and live tarot readings, participants will examine engines, fluids, tools, and suspension as interconnected systems that reveal broader ideas about labor, care, transformation, and resilience.

No automotive knowledge or tarot experience is required. Participants will engage with an unconventional mix of automotive knowledge, philosophy, and live tarot readings led by Kenya from the first edition of TURBO TAROT.

The four suits of TURBO TAROT correspond to the integrated systems of a passenger vehicle:

Fire / Wands: Engine, Ignition & Electrical Systems
Water / Cups: Fluids & Hydraulic Systems
Air / Swords: Tools & Fasteners
Earth / Pentacles: Brakes & Suspension

Space is limited to 25 - 30 people, so please register to reserve your spot here: https://rsvp.duke.edu/event/a7d45621-7803-4dde-b4cb-df0d6b3ae83a/summary

TURBO TAROT is a new artist-directed project that uses generative AI as one component of an iterative visualization and production process. Kenya developed the project's conceptual framework, automotive-to-tarot correspondences, visual system, imagery, and individual card concepts, using AI tools as one component of the artistic process.

title: Vintage Base Ball Day at the DAP
location: Historic Durham Athletic Park
description:
A day of vintage base ball played at the Historic Durham Athletic Park !

***Any tickets purchased for our 2025 Vintage Base Ball event are valid for 2026!***

The iconic Durham Athletic Park has hosted baseball games since 1926 and was even featured in an iconic baseball film, but Durham’s baseball roots are even deeper. The first century of baseball was marked by racial segregation and separate leagues for black and white athletes at the DAP until the 1950s; however, Duke Homestead welcomes all people to participate and honors the struggles and achievements of the many players over the past century who brought us the Durham baseball culture we know today. Players will wear historic uniforms, follow historic gameplay, and use historic equipment. The games will follow 1860 and 1869 Beadles Rules.

We invite you to connect with the history of this sport, this place, and this community by enjoying an afternoon out at the ball park.

Admission to the game is $10; children under 4 years old will be admitted free. Game tickets can be purchased online through Eventbrite, or in person at the Duke Homestead visitor center, as well as at the gate on game day. Early-Bird tickets for $5 available until 9/21 (online here or at the Duke Homestead visitor center).

Enjoy a family-friendly day at the ball park complete with “old fashioned” concessions, food, beer, and historic music. Spectators are encouraged to come dressed in your favorite historical, vintage, or retro inspired outfits. We believe in vintage style, not vintage values! Kids will get to play historic games with our costumed interpreters, as well as have the opportunity to run the bases in-between ball games.

Joining our local Duke Homestead team this year will be The Shiners from Rockingham, VA and a special team from the Durham Fire Department! The first game will be played at 11am, with games at 12:30pm and 2pm to follow.

This game is a fundraiser for the Duke Homestead State Historic Site and it is sponsored by the Duke Homestead Education and History Corporation (the site’s volunteer, non-profit support organization), Measurement, Inc., and Stone Brothers & Byrd.

Free parking available at the lot at 412 Morris St, Durham, NC 27701. A couple of handicap spaces are available in the DAP parking lot.

**We are unable to offer refunds on purchased tickets. All cancelled tickets will be considered a donation to the site and will be used for future educational programming.**

title: Open Studio: Glass & Other
location: Fusion Gallery, 321 W Main St, Durham, 27701, United States
description:
Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM. 
Use our studio space and tools or bring your own project to work on; perfect for artists who don’t have a home studio or simply want dedicated time and space to make. Personal cubbies are also available to store works-in-progress between visits. 
Online registration or sign-up via email is required before coming in. Drop-ins are not permitted at this time. If you’d like to come in at a time you don’t see available online, email us at info@fusionnc.com. 
How Open Studio Works
Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction. You should already have the skills needed to safely work in your chosen medium. It’s also a great opportunity to finish projects started during a Fusion class. 
Your Day Pass includes access to our shared workspace, tools, equipment, and currently available non-consumable materials. Consumable and specialty materials are charged separately based on usage. 
Stained & Fused Glass
Prior stained or fused glass experience is required to use our glass tools. Taking a basics or beginner class at Fusion is recommended, but previous instruction at Carolina Stained Glass or Say It With Glass is also accepted. 
• Glass, solder, foil, and frit: $35/lb
• Bringing your own stained glass? Foil and solder use: $6
• Paper stained glass patterns: Free
• Vinyl-cut patterns: $3 each
• An assortment of stained glass patterns is available for studio use
• Kiln firings are handled by Fusion staff only 
Silver Clay
Prior silver clay experience is required to use silver clay tools. Taking a beginner class at Fusion is recommended before using the studio independently. 
• Silver clay: $7/gram prior to firing
• Firing of your completed piece is included and will be completed at the convenience of Fusion studio staff
• Guests may not fire their own pieces without prior authorization from Fusion’s owners 
Drawing & Painting
No prior class or experience is required for drawing or painting. Your Open Studio fee includes access to currently available shared drawing and painting materials. 
Please Note
• Day Pass access is valid 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected date only
• Online or email registration is required before arriving—no walk-ins
• Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction
• Some specialty tools, equipment, or processes may require prior approval or demonstrated experience
• Guests are responsible for cleaning their workspace and helping maintain a respectful shared environment
• Misuse of the space, tools, or equipment or failure to follow studio guidelines may result in removal from the studio without refund

title: Screen/Society--"A Better Tomorrow" (John Woo, 1986) | new 4K restoration
location: Rubenstein Arts Center, Film Theater
description:
New 4K restoration celebrating the 40th anniversary of John Woo's landmark action classic!

"A Better Tomorrow"
(John Woo, 1986, 95 min, Hong Kong, Cantonese with English subtitles, DCP)

A reforming ex-gangster tries to reconcile with his estranged policeman brother, but the ties to his former gang are difficult to break.

The box-office sensation that established director John Woo as the king of 1980s Hong Kong action cinema and set the standard for the heroic bloodshed genre, this electrifying gangster saga combines the director's intricate bullet play with operatic emotion as it tracks the explosive relationship between two brothers, one a criminal trying to reform (Ti Lung), the other a fledgling graduate of the HK police academy (Leslie Cheung) who blames his brother for their father's death. The plot revolves around the split when the younger brother learns the other is a criminal and the efforts of the criminal brother to reform. Along the way are plenty of heists, double-crosses, and shoot outs, and in the first of his celebrated collaborations with Woo, Chow Yun-fat radiates his matchless cool as a hit man who lives by his own code.

"After an up and down decade as a director for hire, working alternately in the wuxia and wacky comedy genres, John Woo finally hit it big in 1986 when he teamed up with Tsui Hark and the Cinema City studio to remake Patrick Lung Kong's 1967 drama THE STORY OF A DISCHARGED PRISONER. One of the most influential films of the past 30 years, A BETTER TOMORROW established the formal and thematic template for a new era of crime movie: everything that has followed, from Woo's follow-up masterpieces THE KILLER and HARD-BOILED to the Triad films of Johnnie To to myriad international imitators. ... The advanced techniques of the Hong Kong action cinema translated from the period kung fu and wuxia film to the modern world of cops and robbers, from swordplay to gunplay.... Precision cutting and flowing camera movement would come to define the action film, blowing away the tension-based American system with a surfeit of bullets, preferably fired by a man clenching a matchstick in his teeth, firing two handguns at once in a vain attempt at exorcising his existential pain." -- Sean Gilman, The Chinese Cinema

title: Fortune Feimster
location: DPAC Presented by First Horizon, 123 Vivian St / William V. "Bill" Bell Way, Durham, 27701
description:
Fortune Feimster is a critically acclaimed comedian, actress, and host known for her upbeat style, unique comedic perspective, and infectious energy. She invites audiences into her world where laughter and love reign supreme. 
She recently wrapped production on the Netflix film The Fifth Wheel, starring alongside Kim Kardashian, Nikki Glaser, and Brenda Song, and directed by Eva Longoria. She will next be seen opposite Will Ferrell in Hawk, Netflix’s upcoming golf comedy series premiering in July 2026, and is currently on her national “Takin’ Care of Biscuits” tour. Most recently, she voiced “Nibbles” in Disney’s Oscar-nominated animated hit Zootopia 2, which grossed $1.8 billion worldwide. 
In 2024, her third Netflix comedy special, Fortune Feimster: Crushing It, debuted following the success of her previous specials, Good Fortune (2022) and Sweet & Salty (2020), both of which earned Critics Choice nominations. 
In addition to stand-up and acting, Feimster co-hosts the hit podcast Handsome with Tig Notaro and Mae Martin, which has amassed over 20 million downloads since its 2023 launch. In March 2026, Handsome won the Outstanding Podcast award at the GLAAD Media Awards, recognized for its impact, humor, and meaningful representation. She can also be heard daily on SiriusXM, co-hosting Netflix’s What A Joke with Papa and Fortune. 
Feimster first gained national attention as a writer and panelist on E!’s Chelsea Lately. Her television credits include FUBAR (opposite Arnold Schwarzenegger), The Mindy Project, Champions, and Kenan, with guest appearances on Claws, Nora from Queens, and Life in Pieces. Her film credits include Yes Day, Office Christmas Party, and Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar, along with voice work in The Simpsons, Soul, and Bless the Harts. 
Originally from North Carolina, Feimster now resides in Los Angeles.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

description:

The acclaimed Duke Chapel Choir and Chapel organists lead the music, supplemented by student chamber groups, professional instrumentalists, and visiting artists.

title: NCJSS Welcomes Ayelet Brinn
location: John Hope Franklin Center 230-232
description:
The North Carolina Jewish Studies Seminar welcomes Ayelet Brinn, Assistant Professor at Hebrew Union College's Skirball (Los Angeles) Campus.  Her research focuses on American Jewish history, gender, Yiddish studies, and popular culture. 

Brinn holds a PhD in history from the University of Pennsylvania and master's degrees in history and library science from Indiana University.   She was previously assistant professor of modern Jewish history and associate director of the Greenberg Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Hartford and has held fellowships at the Hadassah-Brandeis Institute, the Katz Center for Advanced Judaic Studies at the University of Pennsylvania, and at Fordham University and Columbia University.

Her first book, A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press, was published by New York University Press in November 2023 and received the the Association for Jewish Studies' 2025 Jordan Schnitzer Award in Modern Jewish History & Culture: Africa, Americas, Asia, & Oceania.  She had also been awarded a summer fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities. Brinn is currently writing a second book, which will examine U.S. censorship and surveillance of the Yiddish press during World War I and the first Red Scare. She has also published articles in such prestigious journals as Studies in American Jewish Literature and American Jewish History on topics that include Jewish American journalism during the beginning of the 20th century and female journalists in the American Yiddish press.

title: Swift Night Out (Charlotte)
description:
Join NCWF, Mecklenburg Audubon Society, and NCWF Charlotte Wildlife Stewards Chapter to meet the most spectacular aerial insectivores, Chimney swifts. These birds spend almost their entire lives flying, hunting insects, and even bathing on the wing. Having lost much of their habitat to development, chimney swifts now rely on brick mason chimneys for survival. As the sun goes down and the swifts make their way home for the night, chat with local conservationists about chimney swift biology, behavior, and conservation. Discover their miraculous fall migration and observe swifts up close using scopes and binoculars. The night will culminate with the spectacle that is many hundreds of swifts chattering while swirling into a vortex before dropping into the chimney. Help us count the birds and contribute to their conservation efforts.

title: Duke Arts Presents: Camerata Nordica
location: Baldwin Auditorium
description:
From one of Europe's premier chamber orchestras comes a group of eight string players for an almost theatrical approach to chamber playing. Standing in a semi-circle, the self-conducted Camerata Nordica octet is "in a class by itself in the way these players so perfectly negotiate the very intricate, most fiercely quick and complex sections" (ClassicsToday.com).   

Genius, youth, and a hint of irreverence - these are qualities shared by Mozart, Mendelssohn, and Shostakovich who wrote astonishingly good works at a young age. A standout from Sweden's chamber scene, Camerata Nordica brings them together, opening with a jocular romp by Mozart, while Mendelssohn's Octet serves as the anchor of the concert. Written by the composer at just 16, the frolicsome, high-energy Octet, spins dizzying interplay between eight independent voices. Considered one of the masterworks of chamber music, the Mendelssohn Octet inspired the other octet on this program, the blazing Op. 11 by 18-year-old Dmitri Shostakovich.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: CEE Seminar - Adaptability through control in robotic and active systems
location: None
description: One of the hallmarks of adaptive matter is the ability to sense and respond to the environment. How can we engineer soft matter systems to exhibit such behavior? In this talk, I will present our recent findings on systems driven by centimeter-scale actuators (electric motors) and nanometer-scale actuators (myosin motors), using methods from control theory to either design function or probe system properties. Such control-theoretical approaches are often exploited in engineering applications. I will instead emphasize how control in active and robotic systems can help physicists better understand information processing, orchestration of function, and adaptability in living systems.

title: Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design, Main Lobby
description:
Visit the Gregg Museum of Art & Design for the opening of the exhibition Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today and a keynote address by curator Jake Newsome, founder of The Pink Triangle Legacies Project. Newsome's keynote address, "Enemies of the State: The Nazi Persecution of LGBTQ+ People," will examine the complex motivations behind Nazi leaders' choice to persecute LGBTQ+ people and to present it as vital to the success of the Third Reich. A Q&A and a book signing will follow the presentation. Please register to attend.

Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today is a traveling exhibit that explores the persecution of queer and trans people under Nazi rule and the long, ongoing struggle to reclaim their histories. Beginning in Weimar Germany’s early LGBTQ+ movements, the exhibit traces how the Nazi regime targeted those deemed “undesirable” and how survivors faced continued criminalization and silence long after 1945. The exhibition will be on display at the Gregg Museum through Oct. 23.

title: Democrats, the Midterms and the Meaning of Patriotism: A Conversation with Rep. Jake Auchincloss
location: Bryan Center Reynolds Industries Theater
description:
An "Independent Thinkers" Conversation with U.S. Rep Jake Auchincloss hosted by Frank Bruni, Duke professor and New York Times columnist

Has the Democratic Party learned the lessons of its 2024 defeats, in terms of not just the contests this November but the future in general? How can Democrats escape Republicans' caricatures of them and promote ideas that transcend partisanship and unite diverse people?

Please join Frank Bruni for a probing conversation - part of his "Independent Thinkers" series of events - with U.S. Representative Jake Auchincloss, a rising Democratic star and one of his party's least predictable and most thoughtful leaders.

Auchincloss, 38, is in his third term in Congress, representing the 4th Congressional District in Massachusetts. He's the inaugural chair of Majority Democrats, a group of lawmakers insistent that the party devote less energy to deriding President Trump and more to developing an agenda that reaches beyond its base. He's a graduate of Harvard and M.I.T. and a combat veteran who served as an active-duty Marine from 2010 to 2015.

Frank Bruni teaches at Duke's Sanford School of Public Policy as part of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media and Democracy. He's also a longtime writer for The New York Times and the author of five bestselling books.

Frank's "Independent Thinkers" conversations with public figures who defy reductive political labels are part of the Provost's Initiative on Pluralism, Free Inquiry and Belonging.

title: Ackland Film Forum: "Set It Off" (F. Gary Gray, 1996)
location: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
description:
Jada Pinkett Smith, Queen Latifah, and Vivica A. Fox anchor this energetic reworking of the heist film. After a series of setbacks leaves four Black women with few viable paths forward, they embark on a string of increasingly audacious bank robberies. Blending humor, suspense, and tragedy, Set It Off captures both the bonds of friendship and the pressures of race, gender, and economic inequality in 1990s urban America. 
This film will be introduced by Professor Daelena Tinnin-Gadson, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. 
It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. 
UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. 
  
About the Series: 
Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. 
As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. 
From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. 
The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Carolina Science Cafe: Who’s a Journalist in the Age of AI?
location: Haw River Tap & Table, 300 E Main St C, Carrboro, NC, 27510, United States
description:
Who’s a Journalist in the Age of AI? 



Theorizing Distributed Journalistic Authority Amid Newsfluencers, Algorithms, and Generative Systems 



Who’s a Journalist in the Age of AI? addresses a critical development in the news media. In this talk, UNC-Chapel Hill’s Hussman School of Journalism and Media faculty member, Deb Aikat, PhD, will discuss how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reconfigures the epistemic boundaries of journalistic authority, credibility, and public verification in democratic discourse.  



Dr. Aikat will discuss how AI is reshaping press freedom at a time when public trust in media has sunk to 28%, according to Gallup’s 2025 survey. He studies the shifting information landscape in the U.S. and India — the world’s oldest and largest democracies — tracing how digital platforms empower people to publish, protest, and participate in civic life beyond traditional newsrooms. 





Designed for adults, Carolina Science Cafe is a free program that explores science topics making national and international headlines, offering the chance to meet the experts behind the work. This special program is hosted at Haw River Tap & Table in Carrboro on the first Tuesday of every month. Light appetizers are available for all attendees. 











About the Speaker











Dr. Deb Aikat is a professor in the UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media. 



A former journalist, Deb Aikat (pronounced EYE-cut), is a tenured full professor in the UNC-Chapel Hill Hussman School of Journalism and Media who is reimagining the future of a free press in the age of AI. 



Aikat theorizes how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the free press as a democratic institution. When Deb arrived at UNC-Chapel Hill in 1995, the internet was still new terrain. He launched the journalism school’s first online course and helped build what would become the university’s online master’s program in digital communication. Three decades later, he’s studying one of the biggest transformations to ever face the news industry: generative AI.  






More about Dr. Aikat








Carolina Science Cafe is produced by Morehead Planetarium and Science Center and sponsored by the UNC Chapter of Sigma Xi.

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

Readers are:
• Allegra
• Baxter
• Sigma

Backup Readers are:
• Anna
• Valerie
• Heather

Deep Backup:
• Dave

***

***We meet every Tuesday at the same time, but alternate between In-Person*** ***and on Zoom. Members may attend both formats, if desired, but readers will be listed separately under the In-Person or Zoom weeks.***

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Oct 7 - Building Composable Vision Workflows in FiftyOne
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
This workshop explores the [FiftyOne](https://docs.voxel51.com/index.html) plugin framework to build custom computer vision applications. You’ll learn to extend the FiftyOne App with Python based panels and server side operators, as well as integrate external tools for labeling, vector search, and model inference into your dataset views.

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 7, 2026
9 AM - 10 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/building-composable-vision-workflows-in-fiftyone-october-7-2026)**

You’ll also automate repetitive tasks by writing custom workflows executing within the FiftyOne environment. Attendees will learn to transform FiftyOne from a visualization tool into a central hub for your vision stack.

What you'll learn:

* **Build Python plugins.** Define plugin manifests and directory structures to register custom functionality within the FiftyOne ecosystem.
* **Develop server side operators.** Write functions to execute model inference, data cleaning, or metadata updates from the App interface.
* **Build interactive panels.** Create custom UI dashboards using to visualize model metrics or specialized dataset distributions.
* **Manage operator execution contexts.** Pass data between the App front end and your backend to build dynamic user workflows.
* **Implement delegated execution.** Configure background workers to handle long running data processing tasks without blocking the user interface.
* **Build labeling integrations.** Streamline the flow of data between FiftyOne and annotation platforms through custom triggers and ingestion scripts.
* **Extend vector database support.** Program custom connectors for external vector stores to enable semantic search across large sample datasets.
* **Package and share plugins.** Distribute your extensions internally and externally
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Oct 8 - MCP, Agents and Skills Meetup Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on MCP, agents and skills.

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 08, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/mcp-agents-skills-meetup-october-8-2026)**

**Designing Multi‑Agent Systems: Sequential, Parallel, and Beyond with ADK**

Multi‑agent systems are powerful but choosing the wrong interaction pattern can quickly lead to fragile, slow, or expensive AI systems.
In this talk, we explore the core multi‑agent design patterns enabled by ADK, including sequential, parallel, and more advanced coordination models. Rather than focusing on tools alone, we’ll look at how to think architecturally about agent collaboration.

You’ll learn:

* When sequential agents are the right choice and when they become a bottleneck
* How parallel agents improve speed and coverage (and the trade‑offs they introduce)
* Common failure modes in poorly designed agent interactions
* Practical criteria for choosing the right pattern based on task, latency, and reliability

By the end of the session, you’ll have a clear mental model for designing multi‑agent systems that are intentional, scalable, and production‑ready.

*About the Speaker*

[Dr Roushanak Rahmat](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roushanakrahmat/) is an Enterprise AI Architect, Google Developer Expert (AI & Cloud), and recognized among the Top 100 Women in Tech (2025). With a PhD in Artificial Intelligence and over 15 years of experience, she specializes in designing and delivering enterprise-scale Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Deep Learning solutions that transform industries including healthcare, finance, energy, and public services.

**Privacy by Deployment: Architecting Agent-Driven Localization Workflows for Regulated Environments**

Most enterprise AI today is private by promise - a DPA, a SOC 2 report, or a contract clause that says, "we won't train on your data". For a regulated buyer, these are remedies after a breach, not controls that prevent or contain one. For organizations in healthcare, finance, defense, and government, privacy often requires stronger guarantees: data residency, customer-controlled execution, and, in some cases, operation within air-gapped environments.

This session demonstrates how agentic AI can automate a localization workflow while operating within these constraints. Using a real-world localization pipeline as an example, we will show how agentic systems can coordinate translation, review, quality assurance, and content preparation tasks while incorporating human checkpoints for approval and oversight.

We will also walk through the architectural patterns that enable these workflows to run inside customer-controlled and air-gapped environments without transferring sensitive content outside the customer boundary. The session includes a live product demonstration.

Key Takeaways

* Architectural patterns for deploying agentic AI in air-gapped and customer-controlled environments
* How agentic systems can automate localization workflows while preserving critical human review and approval processes
* Practical considerations for operating agentic workflows in regulated environments with auditability and governance requirements

*About the Speaker*

[Shruti Joshi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/28shruti) is building an AI powered secure localization stack for regulated industries such as healthcare, legal, finance that cannot send their content to a typical hosted SaaS. She brings 12+ years of engineering and architecture experience to the question this talk addresses: how do you make an agentic AI system deployable inside a regulated perimeter.

**MCP Is the Interface; Skills Are the Operating Discipline**

This talk shows how MCP and Agent Skills work together in practical agent systems. MCP gives agents a standard interface to tools, data, and workflows; skills encode the operating discipline that makes those connections reliable. Using a sanitized field-operations ledger as the case study, the talk walks through source intake, normalized state, uncertainty labels, role prompts, QA gates, and share-safe status drafting.

*About the Speaker*

[Chuck Hernandez](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chuck-hernandez/) is an AI engineering and client-delivery leader with 10+ years across software, data platforms, and enterprise implementation, including 3+ years shipping production GenAI systems.

**Agentic engineering is about good guidance.**

Garbage Inn. Is garbage out? This is true. For many input and output processes. In biological life and in computer systems, and equally true when working with LLM’s. The better the prompt, the better the context, the better the focus, And the better the contextual awareness, the better the quality of the output the LLM’s generates.
This is the governance, art and practice of what we like to call agentic engineering, something I've been practicing over the last year.

*About the Speaker*

[Dimitri Geelen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dimitrigeelen/) builds things that don't need him once they're done. Frameworks, transitions, agentic systems — the measure of success is always the same: does it hold up when he leaves the room? He understands not just how to deploy, but what it takes for a new service to survive and scale inside a complex enterprise.

description:
Two hundred and twenty years after Lewis and Clark documented the animals of the west in their journals, we retraced their route with camera traps to find out what we lost, what’s still there, and what it took to save America’s wildlife. 
Dr. Roland Kays, head of the Biodiversity Research Lab at NCMNS and professor at NC State University, will share the story of his team’s expedition across the United States in this special lecture event. 
Doors open at 6:30PM. The lecture begins in the WRAL 3D Theater at 7PM. This event is free and open to the public. 
About Return of the Wild 
Lewis and Clark’s journals are the oldest wildlife survey of North America we have. Two men writing down every animal they encountered, most of which they’d never seen before. Last summer Dr. Roland Kays led a team retracing their route from Pittsburgh to the Pacific, stopping along the route to set camera traps, drag boats up the same rivers, and talk with the tribal colleges, ranchers, and biologists who live there now. Some of what the explorers described is gone. Some of it is standing in people’s backyards. The difference between those two lists is thanks to national parks and refuges, state wildlife agencies, tribal nations getting their land and their animals back, and a century of publicly funded science keeping track of it all. Come hear which animals made it, which ones didn’t, and how close we came to losing it all. 
About Dr. Roland Kays
 
Roland Kays is a scientist, author, podcaster, and YouTuber, with a broad interest in ecology and conservation, especially of mammals. He seeks out questions that are scientifically interesting but also have real-world relevance through educational or conservation value. He is an expert in using new technologies to study free-ranging animals, especially to track their movement with telemetry, GPS, and remote camera traps. He combines this high-tech work with traditional methods, collecting data through new field work and studies of museum collections.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

description:

The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Roots of Discovery: Sands of Knowledge
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Journey through the rich cultures of the Muslim world and discover an extraordinary legacy of curiosity, creativity and innovation. Explore how scholars, artists and thinkers preserved ancient knowledge, transformed it through new discoveries, and shared ideas that would influence Europe and help shape our modern understanding of mathematics, astronomy, medicine, art, architecture and the natural world. 
Presentations

12:30 – 1pm, SECU Daily Planet Theater
Hearts, Minds, and Healing: How Caring for Others Connects Us All
Caring for others is rarely a one-way exchange; what we extend to others returns to shape us. This session transitions between the heart and the mind. It brings the compassion and service at the center of Islamic tradition into conversation with empathy and self-awareness, the cornerstones of emotional intelligence, and asks how each becomes a form of healing. What emerges is a picture of what encourages individuals make a meaning of their own stories, allows them to feel seen and heard. Recognition, in turn, is what binds a community together 
About the speaker
Fatma Wasel was born in Kuwait, raised in Yemen, and has Egyptian roots. She holds a Doctorate in Executive Leadership focused on emotional intelligence and cross-cultural integration. A U.S. State Department alumna, educator, trainer, activist, and linguist, she has worked across government, nonprofit, and private sectors nationally and internationally. 

1 – 1:30pm, SECU Daily Planet Theater
Healing and Discovery: The Muslim Legacy in Medicine and Engineering
From Al-Zahrawi, the father of modern surgery whose surgical texts shaped European medicine for centuries, to Al-Jazari’s ingenious mechanical inventions, this talk explores the golden age of Muslim scientific achievement in medicine and engineering. Discover how scholars across the Islamic world advanced surgery, pharmacology, and mechanical design in ways that continue to influence science today. 
About the speaker
Mohsen Zakaib is a physician-in-training with a multidisciplinary background in nuclear engineering, business, and Islamic studies. He holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Nuclear Engineering, an MBA, and a bachelor’s in Islamic Studies. Mohsen serves as Director of Development at the Lighthouse Project and co-founded RISE at the Islamic Association of Raleigh. 
Activities
Nature Research Center Lobby
Creatures beyond the Sand: Wildlife Across a Continent 
NC Museum of Natural Sciences
Journey beyond the desert and discover the incredible diversity of animals found across Africa and its surrounding islands. Meet fascinating creatures and explore the unique adaptations that help them thrive in habitats from forests and wetlands to grasslands and beyond. 
Mapping the Heavens: Stars, Time & Discovery
Artist Ummah
Look to the skies and discover how Muslim scholars mapped the stars, measured time and expanded our understanding of the universe. 
Healing Through Knowledge: The Roots of Medicine
Artist Ummah
Discover how Muslim physicians studied the human body, advanced medical treatments and preserved knowledge that helped shape modern medicine. 
The Living Lineage: A Journey into the Muslim Arts 
Artist Ummah
Journey through timeless traditions of calligraphy, geometry, tezhip, ebru, and other contemporary art forms inspired by the classical Muslim arts. Discover how artists across North Carolina are reimagining these rich traditions while honoring their heritage and helping keep these beautiful art forms alive for generations to come. 
Interactive Arabic Calligraphy Demonstration 
Artist Ummah
Experience a live Arabic calligraphy demonstration with local artist, who will showcase the art of Arabic lettering and write visitors´names in Arabic. 
Sips of History: Coffee, Tea & Tradition  
Artist Ummah
Explore the fascinating journey of coffee from its roots in the Muslim world, where it was cultivated, brewed, and celebrated as part of social and intellectual life.  
A Cup of Connection 
Salt & Cheeni 
Enjoy a complimentary sample of freshly brewed coffee with Salt & Cheeni! Discover how the right grind and brewing method bring out the best in every bean, and explore how coffee is more than just a drink—it’s conversation, connection, and comfort in a cup. 

About our Collaborator 
Artist Ummah is a community-driven art organization that uplifts diverse Muslim voices and builds bridges of understanding between communities. To learn more about what they do, visit: Artist Ummah 

Roots of Discovery series offers a meaningful platform where communities can share their stories in their own voice — through hands-on science, artistic expression and cultural traditions — while showcasing the connections between culture, nature and scientific discovery.
